Indeed, if $q$ divides $u^2+v^2$, then $q\nmid v$ implies $(uv^{-1})^2\equiv-1\pmod q$, impossible because $-1$ is not a quadratic residue modulo such a prime; hence $q$ divides both $u$ and $v$, and descent gives an even valuation.

Let $q\equiv3\pmod4$ have exponent $i$ in $n$. If $q$ has exponent $j$ in $m$, then its exponent in $nm^2=a^2+b^2$ is $i+2j$, which is even by the lemma. Thus $i$ is even. Therefore every prime congruent to $3$ modulo $4$ occurs to an even exponent in $n$. By the sum-of-two-squares theorem, $n$ is a sum of two integer squares. (The case $n=0$ is immediate.)
\end{proof}
